Use Direct Cellpose mask generation from Python through spacr.spacr_cellpose.identify_masks_finetune. This API-only workflow has no Home tile or menu entry. Run a stock or custom Cellpose model on TIFF fields through the Python API. Despite its historical identify_masks_finetune name, this function performs inference, not training. Review normalization, channels, resizing and model parameters; masks are written only when save is enabled. Import compatible image/mask pairs through External Masks before Measure, or curate the pairs before training. This call does not build a Measure-ready merged project. Direct Cellpose mask generation reads the TIFF fields for direct Cellpose inference and the segmentation checkpoint. Look for the TIFF fields for direct Cellpose inference here: Top-level, lowercase .tif files in src; existing same-name files in src/masks are skipped. Supply the configured channels and a compatible stock model_name or custom_model checkpoint. From those, Direct Cellpose mask generation produces the direct Cellpose TIFF masks. You'll find the direct Cellpose TIFF masks here: When save=True, src/masks/<image-name>.tif contains integer labels. The call returns None and does not produce merged arrays or measurements.db. Cellpose Workbench can supply the segmentation checkpoint. Pass the trained checkpoint as custom_model with the matching image channels and preprocessing. External Masks picks up the direct Cellpose TIFF masks next. Provide the saved label TIFFs and their original images to External Masks, assign object roles and create the merged project before Measure.

Use Pooled-screen simulation sweep from Python through spacr.sim.run_multiple_simulations. This API-only workflow has no Home tile or menu entry. Use the Python sweep API to explore stated screen-design assumptions. It expands combinations, runs simulations in a process pool and writes synthetic summary statistics; it returns None. Set a small explicit max_workers value and a bounded parameter grid before running. The output does not replace measurements or barcode counts for experimental Regression. Use the findings as planning evidence, with their assumptions recorded. Review the synthetic summaries when choosing planning assumptions; transfer those assumptions manually into Power / Design or Experiment Design. Neither tool imports this simulation database, and neither exports the simulation settings grid. Pooled-screen simulation sweep reads the pooled-screen simulation assumptions. Look for the pooled-screen simulation assumptions here: Python settings dictionary: iterable sweep values for screen size, occupancy, classifier accuracy and sequencing assumptions, plus replicates, src, name, variable, plot and max_workers. generate_parameters expands their Cartesian product; begin with a small sweep and an explicit worker bound. From those, Pooled-screen simulation sweep produces the synthetic screen simulation summaries. You'll find the synthetic screen simulation summaries here: src/<YYMMDD>/<name>/simulations.db; the sweep appends summary rows to simulations and optionally writes plots. These are synthetic performance estimates, not measured experimental hits. Depending on the route, the tables that matter are simulations.

When you know your next task, jump to its chapter and open the linked module lesson for its controls and example data. Keep every output beside the settings that made it. The module pages and the Python API describe the same files, tables and identifiers when you connect steps in your own analysis.

lessons.title: Image analysis modules and how they relate
lessons.description: Choose an image-analysis route through segmentation, measurement, annotation, classification, projections, gates, image registration, quality control and assays.
objectives: Choose a starting module from the data you already have.
Identify what each module reads and writes.
Follow the linked module lessons and API contracts for the next step.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR and open Home. Choose the starting data for your workflow, then follow the linked module lessons for controls and example data.

scenes.narration: Image analysis in spaCR follows your pictures from pixels to answers. Raw images start in Mask, which finds the objects. If you want to correct masks by hand, use Make Masks, or import masks you already have. Measure then turns images and masks into numbers, and crops if you want them. From there you choose the road: classification, image exploration, gating or an assay. Stitch tiles first when the analysis needs one coordinate system.

Raw microscope images begin in Mask. Open it from Home, choose the channels and segmentation models, and check the preview before you run. Mask writes each field as a merged array, the image channels and their integer label planes together, and that merged array is what Measure reads next. Mask also keeps a small counts database, but that is a tally, not a feature table.

Sometimes masks need a human hand. Open Make Masks from Home to correct them field by field. What you save here can go two ways. To train segmentation, curate image and mask pairs and keep them side by side as training fields. To measure, use FEATURES to pair each image with its mask and write a measured project, which is how these masks reach Measure; a standalone mask is not a merged array. Plaque masks drawn here can also feed the Plaque Assay with their matching source images. Saving a mask does not train a classifier.

Measure is the hub of this whole map. Open it from Home and point it at the project Mask built, with the image and mask channel indices set correctly; masks paired in Make Masks arrive here too. Measure reads the images and label planes together and writes every cell, nucleus or parasite as a row in measurements.db. Turn on crop saving if you want a PNG of each object, and keep the database with its source project if you stream crops instead. Almost everything else starts from these rows. Annotate and Classify use the measurements and crops to learn phenotypes. Image UMAP projects them so you can look for groupings, and Embeddings encodes the crops with a model, recording the encoder and channel policy. Gate Editor sets thresholds on the real measured features, in their real units, and QC shows which checks exist and which are missing. The Toxoplasma assays pick up here as well: Recruitment needs the right compartment intensities, the Invasion Assay needs two-colour stain measurements with baseline controls, and the Replication Assay needs explicit parasite-to-vacuole links. Host–Pathogen Analysis wants whole-vacuole masks and host reference intensities, with the uninfected cells kept in. And the Endodyogeny size proxy reads the measured project from Python, once you have checked host-cell aggregation and area units; the Mask counts database alone is not enough.

With measurements in hand, Annotate is where you teach by example. Open it from Home and it shows the object crops Measure saved or streams from the project. Label representative objects; each label goes into an annotation column of the png_list table, tied to that object's identity. You don't have to start from nothing: gates saved in Gate Editor can propose candidate labels for you to review. Use a separate column for each question, keep training and evaluation objects apart, and that column is what Classify trains on next.

Open Classify from Home to turn labels into predictions. It has two families, and your data decides between them. Computer Vision learns from object crops, saved or streamed by Measure; Tabular Machine Learning learns from the measured feature columns. The labels can come from three places. Most often they come from Annotate. Gate Editor can write reviewed gate selections to an annotation column, and Image UMAP can do the same with reviewed lasso selections; either way, select that same column and object population here. An embedding cluster is not ground truth, so inspect the crops, validate the labels and keep validation objects apart from training. Classify then saves its scores, the trained model and an evaluation bundle of held-out predictions. In a screen, pick the CV or ML score column you mean and carry it, plate and well identity intact, into Regression.

Image UMAP is for looking before you label. Open it from Home and it projects the measured features from Measure, or encoder features from Embeddings with matching object IDs, into a map where similar objects sit close together. Open representative crops to see what a region really holds. A cluster is only a candidate grouping, not a validated phenotype. When a region does look meaningful, draw a lasso around it, review what you caught, and write the selection to an annotation column in the matching measurement database. Classify can then train on that column. The projection can also go to Gate Editor, if you would rather define the selection there with the matching coordinate and feature columns. Not every GUI route saves encoder features for you, and a shape on a plot alone does not establish a biological phenotype.

Gate Editor lets you choose objects by rule rather than by eye. Open it from Home and draw threshold or polygon gates on real columns: measured features from Measure, in their actual units, or the coordinates of an Image UMAP projection. Save a gate and you can apply it again to any compatible objects. Its Annotate button writes the displayed gates to an annotation column, once you have reviewed the selected objects and chosen binary or multiclass labels. Saved gates can also propose candidate labels inside Annotate. Then select that same column and object population in Classify, keeping validation objects separate from the training labels.

Some analyses need tiles stitched into one picture first. Open Align & Stitch from Home, check the tile geometry, overlap and channel mapping, and save the mosaic with its coordinate records. For OPS, keep the original cycle and site identities as well.

Now the Toxoplasma assays. Open Toxoplasma from Home and choose Plaque Assay. This one skips Measure: it reads plaque images, or masks you already have, and runs the configured plaque model. Masks from Make Masks work here if they are plaque masks with matching source images; cell masks are not plaque labels. It saves plaque results and masks, and the plaque example lesson shows a full run.

Recruitment asks how much of a marker gathers at the parasite. Open Toxoplasma from Home, then choose Recruitment. It reads compartment intensities from Measure, with matching host and pathogen identities, and computes recruitment ratios that keep each well and condition.

Host–Pathogen Analysis looks at infection from both sides. Open Toxoplasma from Home, then choose it. It reads measurements from Measure that include whole vacuoles, host reference compartments and the uninfected host cells, which form the infection denominator. Select the marker channels and set ratio thresholds calibrated on your controls. If you segmented individual parasites, it can count them per vacuole from explicit links or a measured count column. You then get vacuole, host and well tables, joint marker states, replication distributions and any parasite links it could not match. Unknown measurements stay unknown, and host identity alone never defines a vacuole.

To tell parasites that merely attached from those that got inside, open Toxoplasma from Home and choose Invasion Assay. It relies on two-colour differential-staining measurements from Measure, together with stain-baseline controls, and saves assay results with each well and condition intact.

The Replication Assay, also under Toxoplasma on Home, counts parasites in each vacuole and compares those distributions between conditions. It reads objects from Measure, but it needs explicit parasite-to-vacuole identities; host identity alone does not define a vacuole.

Any time after Measure, open QC from Home to check your work. It reads the stored checks for segmentation, units, leakage and plate effects, and its nested viewers let you look closer. A missing check is not a passing one. QC saves its results with exportable figures and tables.

Embeddings describes objects by what a model sees rather than by hand-picked features. Open it from Home, choose a model and a channel policy, and it encodes the object crops Measure produced into one feature vector per object. Record the object identities, the encoder and the channel policy with those features, because Image UMAP needs a feature table with matching object IDs, and not every route saves one for you.

Two tools in this map live only in Python. The first is the endodyogeny size proxy, spacr.submodules.analyze_endodyogeny; it has no Home tile or menu entry. It reads measured compartment areas from your Measure projects, labels them by condition, and bins area to the power of one and a half into log2 size doublings. By default it sums pathogen area per host cell, not per vacuole, so several vacuoles in one cell are combined. That makes it an area-derived size proxy, not a measured volume or a parasite count; for parasites per vacuole, use the Replication Assay. Set the compartment, area filters, calibration, conditions and grouping before you call it, and check aggregation and area units before reading the bins. The Mask counts database alone is not enough.

The second is direct Cellpose mask generation, spacr.spacr_cellpose.identify_masks_finetune, again with no Home tile or menu entry. Despite that name, it runs inference, not training: it applies a stock or custom Cellpose model to the TIFF fields in a folder. Check normalization, channels, resizing and model settings first, and enable saving, because masks are written only when save is on. What you get are label TIFFs, not a Measure-ready project. To carry on, import the image and mask pairs through External Masks before Measure, or curate them for training.

So the image route nearly always runs Mask into Measure, then branches toward your question. To train your own segmentation model, prepare image-mask pairs in Make Masks, train them in Cellpose Workbench and open the saved model back in Mask. With compatible outputs in hand, step in later. Wherever you go, keep channel identities, units and object keys with each result.

lessons.title: Sequencing modules and how they relate
lessons.description: Connect sequencing and optical barcode workflows to phenotype scores, regression, experiment planning, power estimates, dose-response analysis and run comparison.
objectives: Choose a starting module from the data you already have.
Identify what each module reads and writes.
Follow the linked module lessons and API contracts for the next step.
lessons.prerequisite: Install spaCR and open Home. Choose the starting data for your workflow, then follow the linked module lessons for controls and example data.

scenes.narration: Sequencing is how a pooled screen learns which guide sits in which well or cell, and spaCR reads it two ways. Reads from a sequencer go into Map Barcodes. Barcodes imaged cycle by cycle go into OPS, which lives inside Mask. Either way, the barcode identities end up beside your phenotypes in Regression. Around that core sit the planning tools, Experiment Design and Power, for before you acquire, and Dose–Response and Run Compare for your results.

Start with the sequencing reads. Open Map Barcodes from Home and give it your FASTQ files, single-end or paired, with the barcode reference tables that encode your experiment. Map Barcodes matches each read to its barcodes and counts the guides in every well, saving unique_combinations.csv and annotated_reads.h5 in its run folder. Before you trust those counts, open them in Barcode QC. Once they pass, they are the guide counts Regression pairs with phenotype scores, on the same plate and well keys.

Barcode QC lives inside Map Barcodes, so open Map Barcodes from Home and choose it there. It reads the guide counts you just made and shows mapping depth, coverage, barcode collisions and positional effects. It saves the QC results with exportable figures and tables, so you can decide which guides to filter before going further.

Optical screens take a different road. Open Mask from Home, then choose OPS. Instead of reads, OPS takes the images from each sequencing cycle, aligns them to the phenotype images and decodes a barcode for every nucleus. The results land in the OPS measurements.db, with tables for geometry, phenotype alignment, nuclei and barcodes. That database is not a FASTQ count table, though. To use it in Regression, first join and aggregate the decoded identities with your phenotype data, so each object or well carries both.

Whichever way you sequenced, barcodes meet phenotypes in Regression. Open it from Home. For a pooled screen, it takes phenotype scores from Classify and guide counts from Map Barcodes. For an optical screen, it takes the decoded OPS objects once you have joined and aggregated them yourself; that is not a direct file handoff. It can also model a directly measured response. In every case, plate and well identifiers must agree across the inputs. Choose the response and the controls, run the fit, and read the diagnostics before you call anything a hit. The results folder it writes, with coefficients, hit tables, settings and figures, is what Run Compare opens when you want to line this run up against another.

Now step back to before the experiment. Open Power / Design from Home to estimate how much sampling you need to see an effect, based on the effect sizes and variability you choose. Pilot measurements can support those assumptions, but they are optional. The layout from Experiment Design feeds these estimates, and the estimates in turn may send you back to revise that design.

Open Experiment Design from Home to lay out the plates before you acquire anything. Enter the conditions, controls, replicates and plate constraints, with your power estimates in mind, and export the experimental layout. That layout travels far. Power / Design uses it to set sampling assumptions, and later, once the experiment is acquired and measured, Dose–Response uses its dose and condition identities, so keep them unchanged all the way through.

Dose–Response answers how much, not which guide, so it needs no sequencing at all. Open it from Home and bring your measured responses with the dose and condition identities from Experiment Design. Set the dose and response columns, controls and units, then fit the curves. It saves assay results with figures and tables to export.

Once you have more than one analysis, open Run Compare from Home. It reads your saved run records and Regression results and sets their settings, counts and hit lists side by side. If the input data changed between runs, the differences are not a controlled model comparison, so read them with that in mind.

One more planning tool lives only in Python: the pooled-screen simulation sweep, spacr.sim.run_multiple_simulations, with no Home tile or menu entry. You give it a settings dictionary of assumptions, such as screen size, occupancy, classifier accuracy and sequencing. It expands every combination, simulates each in a process pool and appends synthetic summary rows to simulations.db; the call itself returns None. Keep the parameter grid small and set max_workers explicitly before you run it. What comes out is planning evidence, not data, and it cannot stand in for measurements or barcode counts in Regression. Read the summaries, record your assumptions, and carry them by hand into Power / Design or Experiment Design, since neither tool imports the simulation database.

So the barcode side of a screen always ends the same way: identities joined to phenotypes by plate and well. Keep barcode references and plate layouts with your count tables, and for an optical screen, join the decoded objects to their phenotypes and aggregate them before Regression. The linked module lessons show the settings and outputs for each step.

lessons.prerequisite: Open spaCR Home. The organism guide requires no input files. Each assay has its own inputs and linked walkthrough.

scenes.narration: Every Toxoplasma experiment can start from one page. From Home, choose Toxoplasma: the organism guide, a cell diagram and the available assays sit side by side, ready to explore before you load any images.
Begin with the introduction in the information pane. Each pane scrolls on its own, and dragging the divider gives the guide or the assay tiles more room.
The diagram is there to explore. Hover over a cell component and its description appears. Select several to keep them highlighted, and Clear components resets the picture.

Pick the tile that matches your question. Plaque Assay counts plaques and measures their areas; Invasion Assay asks how many parasites got inside. Recruitment measures how much marker gathers at the vacuole, Replication Assay how many parasites each vacuole holds, and Host–Pathogen ties vacuoles to their host cells. Each has its own lesson.

Let's follow one of them. Click Host–Pathogen and its analysis screen opens. Load test data brings in the supplied microscopy example, and from there the Host–Pathogen tutorial walks you through the settings, preview and Run.

Back on the Toxoplasma page, Starplast opens a knowledge map in its own application; the first time, it offers installation steps to follow. The reference links, meanwhile, open organism resources in your browser.

The guide writes no analysis files, so the real work happens elsewhere. If your images still need segmenting or measuring, return Home first; once the images or tables are ready, the assay pages take over.

lessons.title: Host–Pathogen: link vacuole markers and parasite counts
lessons.description: Load the microscopy example, choose marker and count inputs, inspect the preview, and export linked vacuole, host-cell and well summaries.
objectives: Load the example project and identify the host and vacuole measurements.
Choose marker channels and inspect vacuole-level recruitment in Live preview.
Run the analysis and read the output tables with the correct denominators.
lessons.prerequisite: Use Load test data for the supplied THP-1 microscopy example, or select a measured project with host cells, vacuoles and host-reference intensities. Retain uninfected host cells during Measure when you need an infection denominator. Individual parasite counts require a linked parasite table or a measured count column.

scenes.narration: Host–Pathogen ties every vacuole's markers and parasite count back to its host cell and its well. To get there, open Toxoplasma from Home, then choose Host–Pathogen.

The easiest way in is the example. Load test data downloads a small microscopy project and fills in the settings: two fields with images, host and vacuole masks, and measurement tables. Practise here before switching to your own measured project.

Everything the module reads comes through Source, which should point at the project holding measurements/measurements.db. It can also read a database directly, or combine several projects while keeping each one's identity separate.

Now tell it where vacuoles and hosts live in that database: the vacuole table and its intensity-column prefix, then the host-reference table and its prefix. The example uses pathogen and cytoplasm. The object links connect each vacuole to its host cell, so check they are right.

Marker channels says which intensities to compare, counted from zero. The example picks channel one, the RNF213 marker. Whatever you pick needs intensity measurements in both the vacuole and the reference compartment, because the ratio is built from the two.

At first, leave Marker thresholds empty and simply look at the recruitment ratios. Once your controls show where positive begins, enter the channel number and that ratio threshold; anything at or above it counts as positive. If a reference measurement is missing or invalid, the state stays unknown rather than guessed.

Parasite counts come from one of two places: a parasite table whose rows link to their parent vacuole, or a count column measured on each vacuole. The microscopy example has neither, so leave both empty here, and its parasite counts and replication readouts stay unknown.

Before running everything, try one field. Turn on Live, choose a field and click Run preview. The vacuole table appears beside the image; select a row, or click a vacuole, to see its marker measurements and any parasite count.

When the preview looks right, turn Live off and expand Actions if it is folded. Keep Save on and press Run. The console prints the output path when it finishes, and the results land in results/host_pathogen inside the first selected project.

The results build from small to large. vacuoles.csv has one row per vacuole: its host link, marker ratios, marker state and any parasite count. cells.csv rolls those up into host-cell infection and vacuole counts, and wells.csv summarises them per well.

Two more tables answer the biology. marker_states.csv shows joint marker states, and replication_distribution.csv the parasite counts per counted vacuole. Parasites without a usable parent link land in orphan_parasites.csv. Keep settings.json with them so your channel and threshold choices travel along.

One last check before comparing conditions: the denominators. Infection fractions use the measured host cells that were kept, so uninfected hosts count only if Measure retained them. Count distributions use only vacuoles with a known parasite count, and unknown never quietly becomes zero.
